turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Wednesday, the ninth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things before we start. A weekend truce over Ukraine that lasted exactly as long as the plane was on the ground.
[curious] Only as long as the plane was on the ground?
Only that long. Two — a jobs number so hot the Fed is back to talking about a rate hike, not a cut.
[wry] A hike. In this economy. And the third?
The third is the fun one. We go down the rabbit hole into handheld consoles that play every game ever made.
[excited] Oh, I have opinions about that one. Save it.
The spine today is the return. Everything we were waiting on last week came back — and mostly said, again.
Ecclesiastes on the cover. Nothing new under the sun. [chuckles] Cheerful.
Start with the world. Last week two American envoys, Witkoff and Kushner, flew Moscow to Kyiv under a three-day pause on strikes against each other's capitals.
The first face-to-face push in about eight months. That's the part that felt like progress.
It was. Here's the rest. The pause expired Monday evening. Within hours Russia hit Kyiv with one of its heaviest barrages of the war. At least two people killed.
[exhales] So the falsification test the desk set — does the pause outlive the plane — it failed the same night.
It failed the same night. Ukraine's foreign minister put it plainly. His ballistic missiles, he said, speak louder than his words on diplomacy.
And yet the read from Moscow was all warmth. A spirit of trust. Talk of joint economic ventures.
[deadpan] Warmth costs the Kremlin nothing to broadcast. Putin still rejected a broader front-line ceasefire, and held to his root causes — Ukrainian neutrality, no NATO.
How do the desks lay the views side by side?
Washington, cautious — substantive talks, a refreshed proposal, but no deal. Moscow, upbeat. Al Jazeera leads with the barrage, not the handshake.
[thoughtful] Three windows, one weekend, three different weekends.
And the sceptic is arithmetic, not mood. A source close to the Kremlin says no deal until Russia holds all of Donetsk.
Which they want by the end of this year.
Which at the current rate of advance analysts put closer to twenty thirty-two. If that gap is real, the refreshed proposal has nowhere to land.
[pause] Six years of gap between the deadline and the reality. That's not a negotiation, that's a wait.
One more from the world desk. The Strait of Hormuz. Iran is preparing to formalise control of the approaches — an exclusion zone outside the strait, and a management deal with Oman.
So not another flare-up. An attempt to turn the crisis into a permanent toll-gate.

Exactly the read. About seven million barrels a day still move through it, because they have to. Brent crude sits at ninety-seven dollars and change, a seven-week high, and oil has added roughly ten per cent over the week.
[skeptical] Though Iran has threatened to close Hormuz for forty years and never sustained it. The strait is its own customer.
Fair. The falsification there — a tanker actually turned back, not just warned. Watch for it. Now the money.
The money. This is the one that touches the portfolio.
August payrolls came in at one hundred sixty-two thousand. The forecast was in the fifties. Roughly three times what anyone expected.
[gasps] Three times? A week before an inflation report?
A week before. And that does something specific. It drags next week's Fed meeting away from an easy hold and toward a live decision.
Live meaning — a hike is genuinely on the table.
Swaps are pricing the odds of a rate rise at around sixty per cent. Under a Warsh-led Fed that keeps saying sticky prices worry it more than a soft jobs market.
So walk me through the chain. Hot jobs, then what?
Hike risk lifts the ten-year Treasury yield to four point eight per cent — the highest since October two thousand twenty-three. Real yields firm. The dollar bids back above ninety-nine.
And that's the headwind for everything else.
It caps equities. It pulls gold off its record, down toward four thousand three hundred sixty-eight dollars an ounce. Add the Hormuz premium on oil and you've got a faintly stagflationary mix.
[thoughtful] Inflation arguing for higher rates, growth arguing against. The Fed caught in the middle.
Risk assets took the hint. Singapore's Straits Times Index slipped about half a per cent. Bitcoin fell with them, toward seventy-nine thousand dollars.
Bitcoin trading like a risk asset this week, not a haven.
Not a haven this week. The whole thing turns on Friday's inflation print. If it lands soft, all of today's hike bets unwind as fast as they built.
[wry] So the honest headline is — we don't know yet. Which is the whole issue, really.
That's the spine. And this is education, not advice, as ever. Now — same morning, closer to home. Singapore.
The relief payout. That landed today.
Today. Four hundred to six hundred dollars, to more than two point four million adults. Automatic, if you linked your identity card to PayNow.
And overhead, the haze that won't quite clear.
It broke a hundred on the pollution index last week for the first time since October twenty twenty-three. It eased, then declined to leave. Fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan.
[deadpan] The relief cheque the government can time to the day. The haze it can only forecast.
Nicely put. And one more, with a raised eyebrow attached. Parliament handed itself a pay rise the same week.
[chuckles] The same week as the payout. The timing writes its own commentary.
Ministers up to nine per cent; the member's allowance climbing to eighteen thousand five hundred a month from mid-October. The official line is the committee is independent.
Right. Take me to the chips. This one's a story.

It is. A New York Times investigation says roughly five point six billion dollars of advanced tech — more than three billion of it in Nvidia's latest Blackwell servers — reached Chinese customers through a California firm.
[curious] Reached them how? The chips are banned.

Here's the trick. The firm is called Aivres. It's the renamed American arm of Inspur, which was blacklisted in twenty twenty-three. Same offices, same staff, a new name — and it kept buying the chips legally.
[scoffs] So you blacklist a company and it just changes its letterhead.
Changes its letterhead. It lands three weeks before Xi Jinping visits the White House, so chip enforcement becomes a live bargaining chip.
And the think-tank verdict on the controls?

The Council on Foreign Relations calls the whole regime strategically incoherent and unenforceable. Nvidia's own Jensen Huang calls it a failure — says it cut the company's China share from about ninety-five per cent to fifty.
[thoughtful] Friction without effect. The worst of both.
Quick one from the home lab, because it touches the reader's own bench. The models keep getting small enough to run at home. The catch is the memory.
The memory got expensive.
A thirty-two-gigabyte kit of DDR-five is now around three hundred ninety dollars. About five times what it cost a year ago, because the memory makers feed the AI boom first.
[sighs] The models get cheap the same year the memory to run them stops being cheap.
That's the whole story in one line. Now — the wrist. The Kit desk. Motorola came back to the smartwatch.
Motorola? It's been years.

The Moto Watch Ultra. On sale tomorrow, three hundred forty-nine ninety-nine. A genuinely bright screen — two thousand seven hundred nits — two-day battery, Polar training data, its first watch with a cellular connection.
That sounds like a lot of watch for the money. Where's the catch?
The chip inside is from twenty twenty-two. And it runs last year's software while its rivals are on this year's.
[deadpan] So you can replace the strap and the face. You cannot replace the four-year-old brain.
Which for a buy-once reader is exactly the part that matters. Speaking of buy-once — the Atelier. Today's category is sharpening. Whetstones.
[amused] Whetstones. Okay, sell me a rock.
Here's the thing. A fifty-dollar stone and an eighty-dollar flattening plate will outlast every knife in your drawer. The tool outlives everything it touches.
And the grail? There's always a grail.
Japanese natural stones from the Kyoto mines. Some go for two thousand dollars. And the obsessives themselves admit the edge might be — their words — confirmation bias or placebo.
[laughs] So the experts confess the two-thousand-dollar rock might do nothing a sixty-dollar one doesn't.

The apex a home cook actually needs costs about seventy dollars, and everything past a hundred and fifty is craft, not sharpness. In this humidity, buy the splash-and-go stones, not the ones that soak — a wet stone left in its box grows mould here.
That's the whole desk in a sentence. Right —
[warmly] take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[excited] Emulation handhelds! Little consoles that play every retro game ever made. Tell them how it starts.
It starts with a fifty-five-dollar impulse. A Miyoo Mini Plus, the size of a Game Boy, with a screen good enough to make a thirty-year-old game look the way you remember it.
The I-can-carry-my-childhood feeling. And then the ladder pulls you in.

It does. Mid-tier is a Retroid Pocket, around two hundred dollars, playing PlayStation Two and GameCube. The high end runs to a Steam Deck, which the community calls the retro pick — and it isn't close.
And there's a purist tier. The accuracy people.

The FPGA world. The Analogue Pocket rebuilds the old hardware in a chip rather than faking it in software. Two hundred thirty-nine dollars. The community hub, called r-slash-S-B-C-Gaming, runs to about two hundred thirty-two thousand people.
[curious] And it's a whole culture. Firmware, factions —
Custom firmware with names like muOS and Knulli. Factions arguing which chip, and whether you should just buy a used phone and a controller.
[laughs] So what's the catch, Claire, because you always find the catch.
[deadpan] The catch is the backlog you will never play. And the treadmill — a new handheld comes out roughly every month.
Every month. That's relentless.

And here's the confession the scene makes at two in the morning. A fifty-five-dollar Miyoo plays about ninety per cent of what you actually want. The other three hundred dollars buys consoles you rarely load.
[amused] So the whole hobby is one lovely lie — that owning every game is the same as playing them.
That's the desk. Tomorrow's rabbit hole candidates — miniature painting, speed-cubing, and DJing. The reader picks.
I'm voting handhelds again. [chuckles] Okay, culture and the body. Quickly.
Venice. The film festival. The Golden Lion isn't awarded until Friday, so we can't call it. But two films have the longest ovations.
Which two?

Florian Zeller's Bunker, with Penelope Cruz and Javier Bardem — a sixteen-and-a-half-minute ovation, the third-longest in the festival's history. And Martin McDonagh's Wild Horse Nine, fourteen minutes.
[skeptical] Though a long ovation is partly theatre. The cast is in the room, the clock is a press metric now.
It correlates with a Lion more often than not. But wait for Friday. The Good Life — a watch. MING made a worldtimer that fixes a hundred-year-old flaw.
Which flaw?
Daylight saving. Every worldtimer since the nineteen-thirties quietly lies twice a year. This one splits the city ring, so a single click advances only the cities that change their clocks.
[thoughtful] For the price of a good used car. Two hundred pieces, and it's gone.
Two hundred pieces, and MING's runs sell out to its collectors fast. The family desk now — Singapore's expert panel came down against a blanket social-media age ban.
Against a ban? That's the opposite of Australia.
In favour of fixing the features instead. The infinite scroll, the autoplay, the like-counts. About one in six young people here shows signs of problematic use.
[warmly] And the practical line for a parent.
Judge the nature of the hour, not just the number of them. An hour messaging three friends and an hour scrolling a feed of strangers are the same on a chart and nothing alike in a child.
[exhales] That's the one to keep. And fitness — you've got a heresy for me.

[wry] A peer-reviewed one. A big review titled, honestly, Much Ado About Zone Two. It says the easy-cardio gospel — spend most of your time in Zone Two — may not be optimal for a time-crunched trainee.
Blasphemy. So what should the mid-forties reader do?

Mix it. Zone Two for the base, but add one genuine hard session — the four-by-four interval — and keep lifting. The mistake isn't doing easy cardio. It's doing only easy cardio and calling it optimal.
General guidance, not medical advice.
Always. One booking before we close. Bruno Mars — four nights at the National Stadium next April. The pre-sale opens Thursday, the general sale the fourteenth.
[excited] Set the alarm. And the Japan one — sumo tickets.
The Kyushu tournament tickets drop the nineteenth. Weekend seats vanish within the hour. Now — the Long Read. Slow down with me for this one.
[thoughtful] This is the one from Japan. The cancelling thing.
It started with a woman on social media in twenty twenty-four, confessing she was too tired to bathe. She'd switched to dry shampoo. Thirty thousand people liked it.
And that became — a movement?

It became a name. The bath-cancel sphere. And then sleep-cancel, and overtime-cancel — about forty varieties by last September. This year a trade magazine named its grown-up form the hardship-cancel sphere, and called it the theme of the year.
[curious] Hardship-cancel. Meaning you pay to not suffer.
You pay money, or you hand it to an artificial-intelligence, to erase the hardship entirely. And here's why it's an essay and not a bathing story.
Go on.

Japan built its whole postwar identity on endurance. There's a proverb — buy hardship even if you have to. They invented the word for death by overwork. And this is a generation forming named communities around the public refusal to endure.
[pause] The country that most exemplified endurance, learning to cancel it.
One large firm in seven has now had a resignation delivered by a proxy agency — someone you pay to quit your job for you, so you never face the manager.
[exhales] A market for not enduring. And markets don't grow around fads.
That's the argument. And here's the quiet warning underneath it. In the West we argue about artificial intelligence as a productivity engine, a threat to jobs.
And in Japan?

In Japan it's being received as a machine for cancelling suffering. If the first mass use of it, in an ageing, tired society, is not to produce more but to endure less — the demand curve has a shape no one in Silicon Valley is drawing.
[drawn out] Huh. The West is quietly quitting. Japan is doing it out loud, and with a receipt.
That's the line. Nothing new under the sun, the cover said — and then, in a Tokyo suburb, a generation reaches for the one genuinely new thing. A life with the endurance cancelled.
[warmly] Whether that's the future or just this year's product — we'll know when the bill arrives.
We always do. That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
